title: Negotiate Your Allowance
theme: Learning negotiation tactics through a relatable family scenario
description: You're 12 years old and you want a raise in your pocket money. Over 8 rounds, learn real negotiation tactics — anchoring, listening, BATNA, concessions, and more — by negotiating with your parents. Every tactic you try has consequences.
learning_objectives: Understand and apply basic negotiation tactics in everyday life
Learn the difference between aggressive and collaborative negotiation
Practice balancing what you want with maintaining important relationships
how_to_play: Each round teaches one negotiation tactic. Choose how you apply it with your parents. There's no single right answer — but some approaches build trust while others burn it.

glossary_terms.definition: Starting with a high (or low) number to set the range of negotiation in your favour
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — your backup plan if the negotiation fails
Giving up something in exchange for getting something else you want
Bundling multiple items together in a negotiation so both sides feel they're getting more
Fully concentrating on what the other person is saying, not just waiting for your turn to speak

rounds.title: Opening Position
rounds.situation: {player_name}, you currently get ₹200 per week as pocket money. You want ₹500. Your parents are having chai after dinner — the mood is relaxed. Amma asks, 'Is there something on your mind? You've been fidgety all evening.' This is your moment. How do you open?
rounds.story: The way you start a negotiation sets the tone for everything that follows.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family having chai in living room, teenager looking thoughtful, parents relaxed on sofa
rounds.coaching_moment: The opening of any negotiation matters enormously — it frames everything that comes after.

choices.label: Ask directly for ₹500
choices.description: Be upfront: 'Amma, I think I need ₹500 per week now. I'm older and my expenses have gone up.'
choices.consequence_hint: Bold and clear, but ₹500 might shock them and put them on the defensive immediately

events.description: Papa raises an eyebrow. Amma says, '₹500? That's more than double!' The negotiation has started.

choices.label: Start with a question
choices.description: Say, 'I wanted to talk about my pocket money. Can we discuss what a fair amount would be for someone my age?'
choices.consequence_hint: This is respectful and opens dialogue, but you haven't stated what you actually want yet

events.description: Papa puts down his phone. Amma says, 'That's a mature way to bring it up. Let's talk.'

choices.label: Compare with friends' allowances
choices.description: Say, 'Rohan gets ₹400, Priya gets ₹350. I only get ₹200. Can we increase it?'
choices.consequence_hint: Comparison gives you data, but parents hate being compared to other parents

events.description: Papa frowns: 'We don't decide based on what Rohan's parents do.' Amma sighs.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Anchoring Move
rounds.situation: The conversation is going. {player_name}, you need to set an anchor — a number that frames the rest of the negotiation. Papa says, 'Okay, so what exactly do you have in mind?' This is the moment to plant your number.
rounds.story: In negotiation, the first specific number mentioned tends to pull all future numbers toward it.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager holding up fingers counting, parents listening intently at dining table
rounds.coaching_moment: Anchoring is one of the most powerful negotiation tactics — the first number sets the range for everything after.

choices.label: Anchor high: ask for ₹600
choices.description: Ask for more than you actually want. If they negotiate down, you still end up closer to ₹500.
choices.consequence_hint: Smart anchoring, but if the number is too high, parents may dismiss the whole conversation

events.description: Papa laughs: '₹600? You're negotiating like a businessman.' But the number is in the air now.

choices.label: State your real number: ₹500
choices.description: Be honest about what you want. Trust builds credibility.
choices.consequence_hint: Honest and trustworthy, but you have no room to negotiate down — ₹500 becomes the ceiling, not the middle

events.description: Amma nods: 'At least you're being straightforward.' Papa thinks quietly.

choices.label: Let them suggest first
choices.description: Say, 'What do you think would be fair?' Let them set the anchor instead.
choices.consequence_hint: You learn their range, but their anchor might be much lower than yours

events.description: Papa says, 'How about ₹250?' Your heart sinks. That's barely more than what you get.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Listening to Their Interests
rounds.situation: {player_name}, your parents start explaining their side. Amma says, 'We're not saying no. But we want to know — what do you actually need the money for? Last month you spent ₹150 on a mobile game.' Papa adds, 'If we increase it, will you actually save some?'
rounds.story: Good negotiators don't just push their position — they listen for what the other side really cares about.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family in a living room, teenager listening carefully to parents who are explaining something, warm lighting
rounds.coaching_moment: The best negotiators spend more time listening than talking — understanding the other side's concerns is your biggest advantage.

choices.label: Listen, then address their concerns
choices.description: Acknowledge the mobile game spend. Explain your actual needs — school supplies, birthday gifts for friends, bus fare. Show you've thought about it.
choices.consequence_hint: This builds trust and shows maturity, making them more likely to agree to a higher amount

events.description: Amma's expression softens. Papa nods: 'Okay, that makes sense. Let's look at actual expenses.'

choices.label: Defend your spending choices
choices.description: Say, 'It's my money, I should be able to spend it how I want. The point is I need more.'
choices.consequence_hint: This asserts independence but sounds entitled — parents will worry you'll waste the extra too

events.description: Papa's jaw tightens. 'That's exactly the attitude that makes us hesitant.' The mood shifts.

choices.label: Offer to track your expenses
choices.description: Say, 'What if I keep a record of every rupee I spend for the next month? That way you can see I'm responsible.'
choices.consequence_hint: This is a smart concession that costs you nothing but gives them peace of mind

events.description: Amma smiles: 'That's actually a very grown-up offer.' Papa reaches for his phone calculator.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Making Concessions
rounds.situation: Papa says, 'Look, ₹500 is too much. But we can consider ₹350 if you agree to some conditions.' {player_name}, you're at a critical point. You can push harder, accept the offer, or try to negotiate the conditions. Amma adds, 'We also want you to start helping with grocery shopping.'
rounds.story: Concessions are the currency of negotiation — what you give up and what you get in return defines the deal.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family at dining table with notepad and calculator, teenager thinking carefully, parents waiting for response
rounds.coaching_moment: The art of concession is knowing what to give up easily and what to hold firm on — not everything has equal value to you.

choices.label: Push back hard for ₹450
choices.description: Say, '₹350 is still too low. How about ₹450? I'll do the grocery shopping twice a week.'
choices.consequence_hint: You might get more money but parents may feel you're not listening to their constraints

events.description: Papa crosses his arms: 'You drive a hard bargain.' Amma looks uncomfortable.

choices.label: Accept ₹350 with conditions
choices.description: Say, 'Okay, ₹350 works if we can review it in 3 months based on my spending record.'
choices.consequence_hint: This shows maturity and plants the seed for a future increase — smart long-term thinking

events.description: Both parents look pleased. Papa says, 'Now that's a reasonable young person talking.'

choices.label: Negotiate the conditions, not the number
choices.description: Say, 'I'll accept ₹350 but instead of grocery shopping, can I help with something I'm better at — like managing the family's online orders?'
choices.consequence_hint: Creative reframing — you accept their number but shape the conditions to suit your strengths

events.description: Amma laughs: 'Actually, that would be helpful. Papa can never find the right items online.'

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Tension Builds
rounds.situation: Your push for ₹450 didn't go over well. Papa is silent. Amma says, '{player_name}, we're trying to be fair but you're making this feel like a fight, not a conversation. Maybe we should just keep it at ₹200 for now and revisit later.' You can feel the negotiation slipping away.
rounds.story: When you push too hard, the other side can walk away. That's the risk of aggressive negotiation.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager looking worried as parents get up from dining table, tense family atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: In any negotiation, there's a point where pushing harder starts pushing the other side away. Knowing when to stop is as important as knowing when to push.
rounds.timer_narrative: Amma is about to end the conversation...

choices.label: Apologize and reset
choices.description: Say, 'I'm sorry, I got carried away. I really do appreciate that you're willing to talk about this. Can we go back to ₹350?'
choices.consequence_hint: Humility can rescue a failing negotiation — your parents will respect the self-awareness

events.description: Papa sits back down. 'That's more like it.' The tension eases.

choices.label: Use your BATNA
choices.description: Say, 'Okay, if we can't agree, I'll just find ways to earn money myself — tuitions, selling old books, helping neighbours.'
choices.consequence_hint: This shows independence but might feel like a threat — or parents might call your bluff

events.description: Amma looks hurt: 'We're not trying to make you work, beta. We just want you to be responsible.'

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Package Deal
rounds.situation: The conversation is going well. Papa says, 'Okay, let's think bigger. What if we bundle this?' {player_name}, Amma suggests: 'What if we increase your allowance to ₹400, but it now covers your school supplies too? You manage the budget yourself — bus pass, notebooks, everything.' This is a package deal.
rounds.story: A package deal changes the negotiation from 'how much' to 'what's included' — a more creative frame.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family looking at a list of expenses together, teenager writing on notepad, parents nodding, collaborative atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: Package deals work because they let both sides feel like they're getting more — even if the total value hasn't changed much.
rounds.timer_narrative: Papa is ready to finalize if you agree...

choices.label: Accept the package deal
choices.description: ₹400 that covers supplies means you're managing real money. It's more responsibility but also more freedom.
choices.consequence_hint: You learn budgeting for real, and your parents see you as growing up — this could lead to even more trust

events.description: You shake hands with Papa. Amma takes a photo of the moment. 'Our little financial manager.'

choices.label: Counter with a modified package
choices.description: Say, 'I like the idea, but can we make it ₹450 since supplies cost about ₹150 per month and I want some left for myself?'
choices.consequence_hint: A reasonable counter that shows you've done the math — but pushing again after a good offer risks the goodwill

events.description: Papa looks at Amma. 'The kid's got a point about supply costs.' They consider it.

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Emotional Appeal
rounds.situation: The numbers are mostly settled but {player_name}, you sense your parents are still hesitant. Papa says, 'We'll think about it and tell you tomorrow.' You know that 'we'll think about it' often means no. This is your last chance to make an emotional case before they walk away to decide privately.
rounds.story: Emotions aren't manipulation — used honestly, they're a way of showing the other person why something matters to you.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager speaking earnestly to parents in evening living room, emotional but composed, parents listening carefully
rounds.coaching_moment: An emotional appeal works when it's genuine — when it shows why something matters, not just that you want it.
rounds.timer_narrative: Papa is getting up from the sofa...

choices.label: Share why it matters to you
choices.description: Say, 'It's not just about money. When I can't split a bill with friends or buy a birthday gift, I feel embarrassed. I want to learn to handle money, not just get more of it.'
choices.consequence_hint: This is honest and vulnerable — parents respond to genuine feelings more than arguments

events.description: Amma's eyes soften. Papa sits back down. 'We didn't realize it was about that.'

choices.label: Promise results
choices.description: Say, 'Give me 2 months. If I can show you I saved 20% of my allowance, then you'll know I deserve it.'
choices.consequence_hint: A commitment with a measurable outcome — hard to argue against, but you'll have to actually deliver

events.description: Papa smiles: 'Now that's a deal I can get behind. Show us the savings and we'll revisit.'

choices.label: Let it go — don't push
choices.description: Say, 'Okay, take your time. I trust you to be fair.' Walk away and let them decide.
choices.consequence_hint: Showing you can walk away is powerful — but you lose control of the outcome

events.description: You go to your room. At breakfast the next morning, Amma slides an envelope across the table.

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Surprise Counter-Offer
rounds.situation: Next morning, Papa says, '{player_name}, we thought about it. Here's our offer: ₹350 per week, but you earn an extra ₹50 for each chore you complete — max 3 chores per week. So your ceiling is ₹500.' This is a performance-based model you didn't expect.
rounds.story: Sometimes the other side comes back with something you never considered. The best negotiators adapt.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager at breakfast table, parents presenting a written proposal on a notepad, morning light
rounds.coaching_moment: The best negotiations end with a deal neither side originally proposed — that's how creative problem-solving works.
rounds.timer_narrative: Papa needs your answer before he leaves for work...

choices.label: Accept enthusiastically
choices.description: This is creative, fair, and gets you to ₹500 if you put in effort. Say yes immediately.
choices.consequence_hint: You lock in a good deal and show that you value their creative thinking — great for the relationship

events.description: You shake Papa's hand. Amma writes the chore list. It feels like a real grown-up agreement.

choices.label: Negotiate the chore list
choices.description: Say, 'I like the structure. Can I suggest which chores? I'd rather do dishes and online orders than cleaning bathrooms.'
choices.consequence_hint: Smart — you accept the framework but shape the details to suit you

events.description: Amma: 'Fair enough, but bathroom cleaning stays once a week. Deal?' You both laugh.

choices.label: Ask for ₹400 base instead of ₹350
choices.description: Say, 'I love the chore idea. But can the base be ₹400? That way even in a busy exam week when I can't do chores, I'm not stuck at ₹350.'
choices.consequence_hint: Logical reasoning, but pushing again after they made a creative offer might seem ungrateful

events.description: Papa sighs. 'We gave you a good deal and you're already renegotiating.' Amma shakes her head.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: The Final Agreement
rounds.situation: It's Sunday evening. {player_name}, your parents want to finalize everything. Papa has written the terms on a piece of paper. Before signing, Amma asks: 'One last thing — what happens if you overspend one week? We need a rule for that too.' This is the last piece of the negotiation.
rounds.story: The best agreements anticipate problems before they happen. How you handle the 'what if it goes wrong' question shows your maturity.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family sitting together at table, written agreement on paper, teenager about to sign, warm family moment
rounds.coaching_moment: The sign of a truly good agreement is that both sides know what happens when things go wrong — not just when they go right.
rounds.timer_narrative: Papa is holding the pen out for you...

choices.label: Suggest a simple rule
choices.description: 'If I overspend, the extra comes out of next week's allowance. I deal with the consequences myself.'
choices.consequence_hint: Clean, accountable, and shows you're willing to face the downside — parents will be impressed

events.description: Papa writes it down and signs. Then you sign. Amma takes a photo. 'Our first family contract.'

choices.label: Ask for a safety net
choices.description: 'Can we have a one-time ₹200 emergency fund that I can borrow from if something unexpected comes up?'
choices.consequence_hint: Practical and forward-thinking, but parents might see it as a loophole to overspend

events.description: Amma nods: 'That's actually sensible. But it's a loan, not a gift.' Papa adds it to the agreement.

choices.label: Say you'll figure it out as you go
choices.description: 'Let's not overthink it. If I overspend, we'll talk about it then.'
choices.consequence_hint: This sounds relaxed but leaves a gap that could cause arguments later

events.description: Papa hesitates. 'That's how problems start — no plan for when things go wrong.' He writes a rule himself.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

coaching_moment: Negotiation isn't about winning — it's about finding an agreement that both sides can live with and feel good about.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Negotiate Your Allowance Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 4 rounds of Negotiate Your Allowance. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
